extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and readers interested in principles of poetic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing and evaluating poetry grounded in Poe's 'Poetic Principle'—what themes, effects, sources of inspiration, and compositional attitudes produce true poetical effect. Emphasizes elevation of the soul, appropriate use of artifice, and the distinction between antique flavor and genuine merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Principle (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poetic Principle is 'strictly and simply the Human Aspiration for Supernal Beauty.' Its manifestation is 'an elevating excitement of the soul.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poe frames the Principle as the fundamental aim of poetry: to produce an elevating excitement of the soul. This definition is the basis for judging poetic success: does the work express or induce an aspiration toward 'supernal beauty'?

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic effect must be independent of passion and of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The manifestation of the Principle 'is always found in an elevating excitement of the soul, quite independent of that passion which is the intoxication of the Heart, or of that truth which is the satisfaction of the Reason.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poem elevates the soul rather than merely indulging raw passion or advancing intellectual truth. Anti-pattern: confusing emotional intoxication or didactic truth with the poetical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion versus Love: avoid baser passion; prefer true Love (Uranian)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In regard to passion, alas! its tendency is to degrade rather than to elevate the Soul. Love, on the contrary—Love—the true, the divine Eros—the Uranian ... is unquestionably the purest and truest of all poetical themes.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a thematic criterion, prefer depictions of elevated, spiritualized love over violent or merely sensual passion. Poe distinguishes a purer, idealized love as the most fitting subject for poetic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth serves harmony; harmony (not truth) produces the poetical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘If, to be sure, through the attainment of a truth we are led to perceive a harmony where none was apparent before, we experience at once the true poetical effect; but this effect is referable to the harmony alone, and not in the least degree to the truth which merely served to render the harmony manifest.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating the use of factual or philosophical truth in poetry, ask whether it produces perceived harmony. The poetical value lies in the harmonious perception evoked, not in the propositional truth itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources/elements that induce the poetical effect (sensory and ideal list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poe enumerates many simple elements that 'induce in the Poet himself the poetical effect': bright orbs of Heaven, the volutes of the flower, clustering of low shrubberies, waving grain-fields, slanting eastern trees, blue mountain distances, grouping of clouds, twinkling brooks, gleaming rivers, repose of sequestered lakes, star-mirroring depths of lonely wells, songs of birds, harp of Bolos, sighing night-wind, repining forest voice, surf, fresh breath of woods, scent of violet, perfume of hyacinth, suggestive odour from distant islands, noble thoughts, unworldly motives, holy impulses, chivalrous deeds, beauty and qualities of woman (step, eye, voice, laughter, endearments, charities, devotional endurances, faith, purity, strength, majesty of her love).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete sensory images, natural scenes, noble thoughts and unworldly motives are practical sources of the 'ambrosia' the poet uses. When composing or judging poetry, consider whether these kinds of elements are used to awaken the elevating excitement of the soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of frankness and artlessness in certain schools
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The old English muse was frank, guileless, sincere, and although very learned, still learned without art. ... They used little art in composition. Their writings sprang immediately from the soul—and partook intensely of that soul’s nature.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poe praises spontaneous, soul-driven composition for its directness and sincerity. As a positive criterion, unforced naturalness can be a mark of poetic authenticity. But this is not an absolute endorsement of lack of craft (see warnings below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of unbridled abandon: avoid mixing great fire with bathos
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Nor is it difficult to perceive the tendency of this abandon—to elevate immeasurably all the energies of mind—but, again, so to mingle the greatest possible fire, force, delicacy, and all good things, with the lowest possible bathos, baldness, and imbecility, as to render it not a matter of doubt that the average results of mind in such a school will be found inferior to those results in one (ceteris paribus) more artificial.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a balancing criterion: while spontaneity can elevate, lack of art or control risks producing bathos and uneven results. Judges and writers should watch for mixtures of sublime elements with crude or trivial passages and prefer consistent workmanship over erratic extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate antique quaintness with poetical merit
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘At least one-third of the affection with which we regard the elder poets ... should be attributed to the simple love of the antique ... this quaintness is ... a very powerful adjunct to ideality, but ... it arises independently of the author's will, and is altogether apart from his intention.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating old or archaic verse, separate the effect of antiquarian charm (‘quaintness’) from genuine poetic quality. Anti-pattern: praising a poem solely because it feels antique or quaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection and criticism should be discerning, not indiscriminate enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Poe criticizes selections (e.g., the 'Book of Gems') and editors whose enthusiasm is 'too general and too vivid not to be false,' and objects to dignifying 'a series ... of elaborate and threadbare compliments' with the sacred name of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curators and critics should avoid overgeneralized praise and should not elevate merely antique or conventional verse to undue status. Selections should aim to show a school's true character and avoid endorsing threadbare or insincere verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of motive: poetry should arise from passion, not from purpose or commercial aims
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Preface: 'With me poetry has been not a purpose, but a passion; and the passions should be held in reverence: they must not—they can not at will be excited, with an eye to the paltry compensations, or the more paltry commendations, of man-kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a compositional and evaluative standard, authenticity of feeling and motive matters: poetry written primarily for reward, fame, or calculation is less likely to produce true poetical effect. Favor works that arise from genuine passion.
